pos: n. (proper name; a descendant of Ephraim)
etymology: Hebrew 'El'adah, God has adorned, from 'el, God, and 'adah, to adorn, to deck.
biblical_def: Eladah is a man of Ephraim in a line that runs through tragedy: “And the sons of Ephraim; Shuthelah, and Bered his son, and Tahath his son, and Eladah his son, and Tahath his son” (1 Chronicles 7:20). The verses that follow record a raid in which the men of Gath slew Ephraimites “because they came down to take away their cattle” (1 Chronicles 7:21), and the patriarch Ephraim himself mourned many days. Whether the raid is told of Ephraim's own sons in Egypt-era Canaan or of later descendants is debated; the Chronicler's point is the grief and its answer. Ephraim went in to his wife and she bore a son, “and he called his name Beriah, because it went evil with his house” (1 Chronicles 7:23), and from that line came Joshua the son of Nun. Eladah, God has adorned, stands in the list just before the sorrow and the new beginning. The house God adorned was stripped by violence, and God rebuilt it to produce the man who led Israel into Canaan.

corruption_paragraphs: A therapeutic culture wants grief resolved and moved past. The Chronicler records that Ephraim mourned many days and that his brethren came to comfort him, a picture of mourning borne in company and taken to God.

pos: n. (proper name; an Ephraimite slain by the men of Gath)
etymology: Hebrew 'El'ad, God has testified or God is witness, from 'el, God, and 'ud, to testify.
biblical_def: Elead is one of the Ephraimites killed in a cattle raid: “And Zabad his son, and Shuthelah his son, and Ezer, and Elead, whom the men of Gath that were born in that land slew, because they came down to take away their cattle” (1 Chronicles 7:21). Ezer and Elead went down against the men of Gath, the native Philistine or pre-Philistine inhabitants, and died. The text does not excuse the raid; it records it and records the grief that followed: “And Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brethren came to comfort him” (1 Chronicles 7:22). The episode is the background of the name Beriah, “because it went evil with his house” (1 Chronicles 7:23). Elead's name, God is witness, is fitting for a man whose death is preserved without commentary. God saw the raid and the slaughter and the father's mourning, and He recorded them. Out of that evil hour came a new son and, in time, Joshua.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite whose sons built Ono and Lod)
etymology: Hebrew 'Elpa'al, God has wrought, from 'el, God, and pa'al, to do, to make.
biblical_def: Elpaal is a Benjamite, son of Shaharaim by his wife Hushim: “And of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal” (1 Chronicles 8:11). His sons were builders and settlers: “The sons of Elpaal; Eber, and Misham, and Shamed, who built Ono, and Lod, with the towns thereof” (1 Chronicles 8:12). Lod is the Lydda of the New Testament, where Peter healed Aeneas, and Ono lay nearby in the plain where Sanballat later tried to lure Nehemiah. More of Elpaal's sons are listed a few verses on: “Ishmerai also, and Jezliah, and Jobab, the sons of Elpaal” (1 Chronicles 8:18), heads of fathers who dwelt in Jerusalem. Elpaal's name, God has wrought, fits a man whose household built towns. The Chronicler's Benjamite lists, which end in the house of Saul, also record these ordinary builders, for the tribe was more than its one tragic king.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite of Saul's house, ancestor of the archers of Ulam)
biblical_def: Eshek is a descendant of king Saul through Jonathan, the brother of Azel, in the long Benjamite line of 1 Chronicles 8: “And the sons of Eshek his brother were, Ulam his firstborn, Jehush the second, and Eliphelet the third” (1 Chronicles 8:39). His descendants became renowned warriors: “And the sons of Ulam were mighty men of valour, archers, and had many sons, and sons' sons, an hundred and fifty. All these are of the sons of Benjamin” (1 Chronicles 8:40). Benjamin was famous for its fighting men, the left-handed slingers of Judges 20 and the archers who came to David at Ziklag. That Saul's line, after the disaster of Gilboa, should end the chapter with a house of a hundred and fifty archers is a mercy. The house of Saul was not extinguished; it survived in Jonathan's descendants, and Eshek's branch flourished. Jonathan's covenant with David bore fruit for generations.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite chief who dwelt in Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eli'eynay, toward God are my eyes, from 'el, God, and 'ayin, eye.
biblical_def: Elienai is a Benjamite named among the sons of Shimhi: “And Elienai, and Zilthai, and Eliel” (1 Chronicles 8:20), and the list closes, “And Adaiah, and Beraiah, and Shimrath, the sons of Shimhi” (1 Chronicles 8:21). The whole section ends with a summary of rank: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). Elienai was therefore a chief of a Benjamite house resident in the capital. His name is a short prayer: my eyes are toward God, the posture of the psalmist who said, “Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net.” The name of the tribe's chief men in Jerusalem preserves the confession of a people whose help was not in its own strength. Elienai is otherwise unknown; it is his name that speaks.

pos: n. (proper name; a Levite ancestor of Asaph the singer)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ethni, my gift or munificent, from 'ethnah, a gift.
biblical_def: Ethni is an ancestor of Asaph, David's chief singer, in the Gershonite line of Levi. The Chronicler traces Asaph backward: “And his brother Asaph, who stood on his right hand, even Asaph the son of Berachiah, the son of Shimea” (1 Chronicles 6:39), and several generations up, “The son of Ethni, the son of Zerah, the son of Adaiah” (1 Chronicles 6:41), until the line reaches “The son of Jahath, the son of Gershom, the son of Levi” (1 Chronicles 6:43). The purpose of the genealogy is to establish that David's singers were Levites by right. Asaph wrote or gave his name to twelve psalms, including the fiftieth, “Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God hath shined”, and the seventy-third, the great psalm of the prosperity of the wicked resolved in the sanctuary. Ethni, my gift, is one of the generations through whom God prepared that gift for His church's worship.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Zophah, of the tribe of Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Charnepher, perhaps panting; some see an Egyptian form, Horus is good. The meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Harnepher is a man of Asher: “The sons of Zophah; Suah, and Harnepher, and Shual, and Beri, and Imrah” (1 Chronicles 7:36). The list of Zophah's eleven sons continues, “Bezer, and Hod, and Shamma, and Shilshah, and Ithran, and Beera” (1 Chronicles 7:37), and the chapter closes on Asher's strength: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men” (1 Chronicles 7:40). Harnepher's name is unusual; some have read in it an Egyptian element, a possible echo of Israel's sojourn in Egypt. Whatever its origin, it stands in the roll of Asher's fighting houses. Asher is rarely prominent in Scripture, yet the tribe's men are counted here as choice and mighty, and a prophetess of Asher, Anna, would one day welcome the infant Christ in the temple.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Heber, of the tribe of Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Chotham, seal or signet, from chatham, to seal; the same Hebrew name is rendered Hothan in 1 Chronicles 11:44.
biblical_def: Hotham is a man of Asher: “And Heber begat Japhlet, and Shomer, and Hotham, and Shua their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:32). Heber was a grandson of Asher through Beriah, and his children head the long Asherite list of the chapter. In the parallel verse 34 the line continues through Shomer; Hotham himself is not traced further, and some take Helem in verse 35 to be his name in another form. The Hebrew name is the same as that of Hothan the Aroerite, father of two of David's mighty men, but the two are different men of different tribes and generations. Hotham means a seal or signet, the ring that marks ownership and authenticates. The genealogies are themselves a kind of seal on the families of Israel, the record by which each house knew whose it was. The chapter's last word on Asher is the number of its men apt to the war, twenty and six thousand, every one of them sealed into his father's house by name.

pos: n. (proper name; the father of Joseph in Luke's genealogy of Christ)
biblical_def: Heli stands at the head of Luke's genealogy, immediately after Joseph: “And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli” (Luke 3:23). Matthew names Joseph's father as Jacob: “And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ” (Matthew 1:16). The two accounts have been reconciled in two main ways. Many Reformed and older Protestant writers held that Luke traces Mary's line, so that Heli was Joseph's father-in-law and Joseph is reckoned his son by marriage; others hold that Heli and Jacob were brothers or half-brothers and that a levirate marriage made Joseph the legal son of one and the natural son of the other. Either way the purpose is plain. Matthew shows the Son of David by legal right through Joseph; Luke carries the line back to Adam, “which was the son of God” (Luke 3:38), to show the Saviour of all mankind. The careful phrase “as was supposed” guards the virgin birth.

corruption_summary: The two genealogies of Christ are paraded as a contradiction; they serve two purposes and are reconcilable, and Luke's “as was supposed” protects the virgin birth.
corruption_paragraphs: Sceptics have long cited Heli and Jacob as proof that the Gospels contradict one another. The church has offered careful reconciliations since the earliest centuries, and both accounts agree on what matters: Jesus is the Son of David, born of a virgin, the Saviour of Adam's race.

The principle to recover is the trustworthiness of Scripture in its details. Where two inspired accounts differ in form, the reader seeks the harmony the Spirit intended rather than presuming error, and Luke's own phrase shows that he wrote with full knowledge of who Christ's Father truly was.

pos: n. (proper name; an ancestor of Christ in Luke's genealogy)
etymology: Greek Esli, probably from Hebrew 'Atsalyahu, the LORD has reserved, or a form of Hashaliah.
biblical_def: Esli is one of the names in Luke's genealogy of Christ between the return from exile and Joseph: “Which was the son of Mattathias, which was the son of Amos, which was the son of Naum, which was the son of Esli, which was the son of Nagge” (Luke 3:25). He belongs to the long stretch of the line that the Old Testament does not record, the generations after Zerubbabel when the house of David had no throne and lived as ordinary Jews under Persian, Greek and Roman rule. Not one of those men reigned; most are known only by this verse. Yet through them God kept the line until “the fulness of the time was come”, when “God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Galatians 4:4). Esli is a link in the chain Luke lays down from Jesus to Adam. His obscurity is the point: the promise to David was kept in the dark centuries as surely as in the bright ones.

corruption_paragraphs: The four hundred years between Malachi and Matthew are often imagined as a time when God was absent. Luke's list of unknown men, Esli among them, shows the line of David preserved, generation by generation, through those years.

The principle to recover is the faithfulness of God through apparent silence. He was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, and every generation of that seed, however obscure, was kept for His coming.
roots_summary: Greek Esli, probably from a Hebrew name; an ancestor of Christ in the post-exilic generations.
roots_lines: Greek Esli, probably from a Hebrew name with Yah.
